Stage 3 · Grammar

When the doer does not matter

One structure for every tense, and one question that decides when to use it.

Read these two sentences.
  • Somebody in Madrid invented the Ostrich Pillow.
  • The Ostrich Pillow was invented to help long-distance travellers.
Why does the second sentence work better in an article about the product?
The passive is not a different meaning. It is a different subject.

The passive does not change what happened; it changes what the sentence is about. Ali Ganjavian invented the Ostrich Pillow is a sentence about an inventor. The Ostrich Pillow was invented to help travellers is a sentence about a product. Same event, different topic — and in most real writing, the topic is what you are trying to control.

English uses the passive when the doer is one of four things: unknown (Over $195,000 has been pledged), obvious (The money is released when the target is reached), unimportant (The pillows are manufactured in Spain), or deliberately left out (A mistake was made). That last case is worth noticing: the passive is the standard way English avoids assigning blame, which is why it appears so often in official statements.

There is a fifth reason, less obvious but very common in good writing: keeping the same subject across several sentences. The building was renovated in 2015 and is now used as a gallery holds the reader’s attention on the building. Switching to the active would force a new subject into the second half and break the thread.

Structurally the passive is simpler than it looks: a form of be in whatever tense you need, plus the past participle. The participle never changes; all the tense information lives in be. Two restrictions follow. Only verbs that take an object can be passive, so happen, arrive, die and fall have no passive at all. And be cannot be dropped, even after a modal or in a perfect form: must be shown, has been shown.

Before you look at the table: the table below runs the passive through each tense so you can see that only be changes. Read down the left-hand column and watch the participle stay still.
The form — be in the right tense, plus the past participle
TenseActivePassive
Present simpleThey make it in Spain.It is made in Spain.
Past simpleThey invented it in 2012.It was invented in 2012.
Present continuousThey are developing it.It is being developed.
Present perfectBackers have pledged $195,000.$195,000 has been pledged.
WillThey will ship it in June.It will be shipped in June.
ModalYou can see it from the bridge.It can be seen from the bridge.
When to use it, and what to do with the doer
ReasonExample
The doer is unknownThe prototype was stolen in March.
The doer is obviousHe was arrested at the airport. (by the police — who else?)
The doer does not matterIt is pulled over the head to take a nap.
The thing matters moreThe Ostrich Pillow was designed in Madrid.
The doer does matter…by its backers. · …by a team in Madrid.

Ask one question: does anybody care who did it? If the answer is no, or if everybody already knows, the passive is the natural choice — not the formal one.

Only add by when the doer is news. Over $195,000 has been pledged by its backers is worth saying. The pillow was invented by somebody is not.

The mistake to avoid. Verbs with no object have no passive: not The accident was happened but The accident happened. Same with arrive, go, come, rise and occur.

The be cannot disappear. Not It made in Spain but It is made in Spain. This is the single most common passive error at this level.

Full grammar reference — the passive

What it is

The passive is formed with the verb be in the required tense plus the past participle. It reorganises a sentence so that the thing affected by the action becomes the subject, and the person or thing doing the action either moves to the end after by or disappears altogether.

What it means, and what it does

The passive is a choice about focus, not a different meaning. Ali Ganjavian invented the Ostrich Pillow is about the inventor; The Ostrich Pillow was invented to help travellers is about the product. English uses the passive when the doer is unknown, obvious, unimportant, or deliberately left out — which is why it dominates news reports, instructions, scientific writing and business English.

When and why we use it

The passive does not change what happened; it changes what the sentence is about. Ali Ganjavian invented the Ostrich Pillow is a sentence about an inventor. The Ostrich Pillow was invented to help travellers is a sentence about a product. Same event, different topic — and in most real writing, the topic is what you are trying to control.

English uses the passive when the doer is one of four things: unknown (Over $195,000 has been pledged), obvious (The money is released when the target is reached), unimportant (The pillows are manufactured in Spain), or deliberately left out (A mistake was made). That last case is worth noticing: the passive is the standard way English avoids assigning blame, which is why it appears so often in official statements.

There is a fifth reason, less obvious but very common in good writing: keeping the same subject across several sentences. The building was renovated in 2015 and is now used as a gallery holds the reader’s attention on the building. Switching to the active would force a new subject into the second half and break the thread.

Structurally the passive is simpler than it looks: a form of be in whatever tense you need, plus the past participle. The participle never changes; all the tense information lives in be. Two restrictions follow. Only verbs that take an object can be passive, so happen, arrive, die and fall have no passive at all. And be cannot be dropped, even after a modal or in a perfect form: must be shown, has been shown.

Typical situations

You need the passive for reports, procedures and instructions, for describing how things are made or done, for news writing, and for any formal or impersonal text where the process matters more than the person.

  • The doer is unknown — nobody knows, or nobody has said.Over $195,000 has been pledged so far.
  • The doer is obvious — naming them would add nothing.The money is released when the target is reached.
  • The doer is unimportant — the process matters more than the person.The pillows are manufactured in Spain.
  • The affected thing is the topic — keeping the subject consistent through a paragraph.The building was renovated in 2015 and is now used as a gallery.
  • Formal and impersonal writing — reports, procedures, academic prose.Applications must be submitted by Friday.
  • Avoiding blame — the doer is left out on purpose.A mistake was made in the calculation.
  • Naming the doer when it matters — by + agent, used in only about one passive in five.The project was backed by two hundred investors.

How it differs from similar structures

Active answers who did it? · passive answers what happened to it? Same event, different topic. Kickstarter funded the project vs The project was funded through Kickstarter.
was made (passive: somebody made it) · was making (active continuous: it was doing the making). The participle and the -ing form are not interchangeable.

How to build it

General: subject + be (in the right tense) + past participle  (+ by + agent)
Present simple: am / is / are + past participle
Past simple: was / were + past participle
Present perfect: have / has been + past participle
Modal: can / will / must be + past participle  ·  Continuous: is / was being + past participle
Present simpleIt is made in Spain. · They are given a discount.
Past simpleIt was invented in 2012. · The funds were raised online.
Present perfectIt has been pledged by its backers.
Present continuousA new version is being developed.
FutureThe prototype will be shown in March.
ModalThe design can be seen on the website. · It must be presented to the bank.
NegativeIt isn’t made here. · It wasn’t funded by a bank.
QuestionWas it funded by investors? · How is it manufactured?
Two objectsThey gave him a loan. → He was given a loan. / A loan was given to him.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Only transitive verbs — verbs that take an object — can be passive. Happen, arrive, occur, die, appear and fall have no passive: The accident was happened is a fixed error.
  • The tense lives in be, never in the participle. The participle never changes. To move a passive into the past you change is to was, and nothing else.
  • By + agent is added only when the doer carries real information. If you would not mention them in the active sentence, leave them out.
  • The passive of a perfect or a modal always keeps be: has been pledged, must be presented. Dropping be is the second most common error here.
  • When a verb has two objects, either can become the subject; English usually prefers the person: He was offered a job rather than A job was offered to him.
  • Do not overuse it. In a piece of B1 writing, a passive in every sentence reads as heavy; use it where the focus genuinely belongs on the thing, not the doer.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • The accident was happened last night. → The accident happened last night.Happen is intransitive and has no passive.
  • It made in Spain. → It is made in Spain.The passive always needs a form of be.
  • The money has pledged by backers. → The money has been pledged by backers.The perfect passive keeps been.
  • It must presented to the bank first. → It must be presented to the bank first.After a modal, the passive keeps be.
  • The pillow was invent by Ali Ganjavian. → The pillow was invented by Ali Ganjavian.The passive needs the past participle, not the base form.
  • A bank loan was took out to pay for it. → A bank loan was taken out to pay for it.Use the past participle taken, not the past simple took.

More examples in context

  • unknown doerOver $195,000 has been pledged so far.
  • obvious doerThe money is released only when the target is reached.
  • unimportant doerThe pillows are manufactured in a small factory outside Madrid.
  • keeping the topicThe warehouse was renovated in 2014 and is now used as a gallery.
  • modal passiveAnyone’s idea can be presented directly to the people who might buy it.
  • continuousA second version is being developed at the moment.
  • futureThe results will be announced at the end of the month.
  • formal instructionApplications must be submitted before the deadline.
  • with agentThe project was backed by more than two thousand small investors.
  • person as subjectThe founders were offered a loan, but they turned it down.

A tip for remembering it

Transform in three steps and you will never lose a piece. 1 Take the object of the active sentence and make it the subject. 2 Put be into the tense the active verb had. 3 Add the past participle. They funded the project → The project + was + funded. Then ask whether the doer is worth keeping; usually it is not.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Passive = be in the right tense + past participle.
  2. The tense is carried by be; the participle never changes.
  3. Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious, unimportant or deliberately omitted.
  4. Add by + agent only when the doer carries real information.
  5. Intransitive verbs (happen, arrive, die) have no passive.
  6. After a modal or a perfect, keep be / been: must be shown, has been shown.

Stage 5 · Main input

The crowd will pay for it

Products used to be made and then sold. Now it is the other way round.

Before you read: crowd-funding lets people pay for a product before it exists.

What proportion of projects do you think reach their target?

Decide first. Paragraph D gives the figure.

The crowd will pay for it

A hat that lets you sleep at your desk raised nearly two hundred thousand dollars from strangers. Most projects are not so lucky.

AThe Ostrich Pillow was invented to solve a problem that no bank would have taken seriously. Its designer had noticed that people who travel a lot get very tired, and that there is nowhere to put your head. The result is a padded hat that is pulled over the head so that the wearer can take a nap almost anywhere. It looks ridiculous, which is part of the point. More than nineteen hundred people paid for one before a single unit had been manufactured.

BThis is how crowd-funding works. An idea is presented directly to the people who might buy it, usually as a short film and a page of drawings. Money is pledged rather than paid: nothing is taken from anyone unless the target is reached by the deadline. If it is, the money is released and production begins. If it is not, every pledge is returned and the project quietly disappears. Nothing is guaranteed to anybody at any stage.

CFor a designer who is short of cash, the attraction is obvious. A bank loan must be applied for, defended and repaid whatever happens; a crowd-funded product is paid for by the people who actually want it. But the real value is often information rather than money. If two thousand strangers will pay in advance for something that does not yet exist, the idea has been tested before a factory is booked. If only forty will, that is worth knowing too, and it has cost almost nothing to find out.

DThe failure rate is high and is not usually mentioned in the success stories. Only around a third of projects reach their target, and reaching it is not the end of the difficulty. Products that were designed in a bedroom have to be manufactured, packed and shipped to thousands of addresses in dozens of countries, often by people who have never done any of that before. Deliveries are regularly delayed by a year or more, and backers are told about the problem long after they were told about the triumph.

EPlatforms have been criticised for this. Their defenders answer that a pledge is not a purchase: backers are supporting an attempt, not ordering from a shop, and that distinction is printed clearly on every page. Critics reply that it is not how the pages are read, and that a page filled with photographs of a finished-looking product is understood as an advertisement whatever the small print says.

FWhat has genuinely changed is who gets to try. Fifty years ago an unusual idea had to be presented to somebody with money, and most such ideas were refused by people who were paid to be careful. Now they are refused, or backed, by the public. The Ostrich Pillow was rejected by every manufacturer its designer approached. Then it was funded in three weeks by strangers, and has since been sold in more than fifty countries.

Written for this course. Platform mechanics and success rates are drawn from published crowd-funding platform statistics and industry reporting.
